text.p: Harold Stassen, perennial presidential candidate and last surviving signer of the 1945 declaration establishing the United Nations, celebrated his 90th birthday on Monday.
About 900 people showed up for Stassen's party, including former Vice President Walter Mondale, former senator and presidential candidate Eugene McCarthy and other elected officials past and present.
Stassen started political life in Minnesota where he was elected governor in 1938 at the age of 31, at the time the youngest governor in U.S. history.
After being re-elected as governor in 1942, he enlisted in the Navy in 1943, fulfilling a campaign promise. His 1942 win was the last time he was elected to a major office.

In the Navy Stassen became an aide to Adm. William (Bull) Halsey, was present at the Japanese surrender in Tokyo in 1945 at the close of the Second World War and personally liberated American prisoners of war from Japanese camps.

Even though Stassen had always been a Republican, Democratic President Franklin Roosevelt appointed him in 1945 as one of eight U.S. negotiators to the talks in San Francisco that led to the founding of the United Nations. He is the only surviving signer of the U.N. charter.
In 1947, Stassen began a grass-roots campaign for the Republican presidential nomination.

He rode a bus to take his case to the people in the few states that then held primary elections, and won more primary votes than anyone else. But he lost the nomination in 1948 to New York Gov. Thomas Dewey.
Stassen unsuccessfully sought the nomination repeatedly over the next 40 years.
He also helped engineer the nomination and subsequent election of Dwight Eisenhower and served that president as White House adviser on international affairs.
He later practiced law in Pennsylvania and served as president of the University of Pennsylvania, returning to Minnesota 1978. He resides at a nursing home in Bloomington, near Minneapolis.
Last year when he offered himself, only half-jokingly, as vice presidential candidate to Bob Dole, saying it would take the edge off Dole's "too old" image.
